title: Row by row methods for semidefinite programming
contribution: Introduces the row-by-row (RBR) block coordinate descent method for SDP: fixing an (n-1)-dimensional principal submatrix turns the PSD constraint into a Schur-complement second-order cone constraint, giving closed-form updates for maxcut and matrix completion, an augmented-Lagrangian wrapper for general linear constraints, and a convergence proof for the log-barrier version.
problem_entry: Cost per iteration rather than iteration count: IPMs need O(n^6) work and O(m^2) memory per iteration, so the authors accept a non-polynomial method whose iterations are much cheaper; direct predecessor is Banerjee-El Ghaoui-d'Aspremont's Schur-complement BCD (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Fix B = X_{i^c,i^c}; X PSD iff xi - y^T B^{-1} y >= nu (rotated SOC), so each row update is an SOCP, closed-form for maxcut (one matvec, Lemma 3.1) and matrix completion (one small linear solve, Lemma 4.1); wrap in an augmented Lagrangian when linear constraints couple rows (pp. 3-6, 11-16).
assumptions: Slater condition (Assumption 2.1, p. 3); convergence theorem for the barrier problem with box constraints, convex f, strict convexity and compact level set (Thm 3.4, pp. 9-10); AL convergence only argued from standard theory (p. 12).
proof_devices: Bertsekas Prop. 2.7.1 adaptation: monotone decrease, strict convexity along a segment forces X^{k,1}-X^k -> 0, then summed per-row variational inequalities give global optimality (Thm 3.4, pp. 9-10)
reinterpretation of the safeguard nu as a log-barrier parameter sigma so the barrier convergence proof covers PURE-RBR-M (Lemma 3.2, pp. 7-8)
3x3 counterexample for nu = 0 and 2x2 counterexample for coupled linear constraints, each placed before its safeguard (pp. 6-7, 10-11)
experiments: Maxcut SDPs on rudy graphs n = 1000-4000 (random and almost planar, 5 seeds each, commands printed) vs DSDP on CPU time and cycles, e.g. R4000-1 DSDP 6274 s vs PURE-RBR-M 36.5 s (rel-obj 5.9e-3) / 261.1 s (4.0e-5); matrix completion p = q = 100-500, r = 10, no competing solver (pp. 16-19).
positioning: Against interior-point methods (O(n^6) per iteration) and as a primal, overlapping-block relative of Banerjee-El Ghaoui-d'Aspremont's BCD; convergence argument borrowed from Bertsekas (pp. 1-2, 9).
writing: Introduction leads with concrete wall-clock claims (4000x4000 maxcut in under 5.25 minutes, p. 1); each safeguard is preceded by a tiny counterexample; low hedging, with informal asides such as Fortuitously and Somewhat surprisingly (pp. 5, 17).
limits_future: Non-polynomial complexity (p. 1); only two SDP classes tested (p. 15); future work on exploiting the SOCP subproblem form (p. 12) and general conic programs with nonnegativity and SOC constraints (p. 19).

method_links.note: Constraint structure (fixed diagonal, sampled entries) makes each block subproblem a matvec, a cubic root or a small linear solve.
Classical BCD and augmented Lagrangian kept, but the change is a reformulation (PSD -> SOC via Schur complement), not a repair under a weaker oracle.
Step 4 pattern: negative example first (nu = 0; coupled linear constraints), then the minimal safeguard (nu > 0; AL wrapper).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: convergence by embedding in an existing framework
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: AL version's convergence asserted from Theorem 3.4 plus standard AL theory rather than proved.
3x3 example (nu = 0) and 2x2 example (coupled constraints) motivate nu > 0 and the AL wrapper.

transferable: Handle a PSD constraint inside block coordinate descent by fixing the complementary principal submatrix and writing the block's feasibility as a Schur-complement SOC constraint (pp. 3-4).
Justify each safeguard with the smallest counterexample that breaks the unguarded method, placed right before the safeguard (pp. 6-7, 10-11).
Reinterpret a numerical safeguard parameter as a barrier parameter so an existing barrier convergence proof covers the practical algorithm (Lemma 3.2, pp. 7-8).
Print instance-generator commands and random seeds for every test problem (p. 16; Table 5.2, p. 19).
coauthors: Z. Wen, D. Goldfarb, S. Ma

quotes.text: Although the computational complexity of the new method presented here is not polynomial, each of its iterations can be executed much more cheaply than in an interior point algorithm.
Fortuitously, the optimal solution of (3.2) is determined by a single matrix-vector product as we can see from the following lemma.

title: SINCO-a greedy coordinate ascent method for sparse inverse covariance selection problem
contribution: Proposes SINCO, a greedy primal coordinate ascent method for l1-penalized sparse inverse covariance selection whose single-entry steps have closed-form exact line searches, and shows empirically that its iterate path reproduces the regularization-path ROC and yields lower false-positive rates than glasso.
problem_entry: Structure recovery of Gaussian Markov networks: COVSEL/glasso work on the dual with whole-row BCD, IPMs are O(p^6) per iteration and recover sparsity only in the limit; judge algorithms by true/false positives, not just objective (pp. 1-5, 11).
key_idea: Update one diagonal entry or one symmetric pair of C at a time; with W = C^{-1} the exact line search is a root of a quadratic, so all O(p^2) candidate steps can be evaluated and the best one taken (Gauss-Southwell), with an O(p^2) Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury update of W (pp. 5-9).
assumptions: Zero-mean Gaussian data (p. 3); nonnegative entrywise penalty matrix S allowing row-specific lambda_i (p. 4); convergence asserted from BCD on a strictly convex objective and the RBR result, not proved (p. 9).
proof_devices: closed-form determinant of a symmetric rank-two update: det(C + theta(e_i e_j^T + e_j e_i^T)) = det(C)(1 + 2 theta W_ij + theta^2 (W_ij^2 - W_ii W_jj)) (pp. 7-8)
root localisation: positive discriminant, f'(0) > 0 and f -> -infinity at theta_max = 1/(sqrt(W_ii W_jj) - W_ij) give exactly one root in (0, theta_max) (p. 8)
experiments: Synthetic random and scale-free networks with known ground truth (p = 100-1100, n = 500-5500) vs glasso on ROC and CPU (implementation asymmetry acknowledged); fMRI StarPlus data (3 subjects, 40 samples, leave-one-out) vs COVSEL and SVM (pp. 9-17).
positioning: Against glasso and COVSEL (dual row-wise BCD) and interior-point methods; presented as a simplified RBR method (S048) applied to the primal (pp. 4-5).
writing: Claims framed around structure recovery (false positives) rather than speed alone; a key weakness (missing true positives on denser networks) stated early (p. 5); convergence handled in one paragraph by reference (p. 9).
limits_future: May miss true positives on dense networks (p. 5); tolerance path costs more CPU than the regularization path (p. 12); may be too slow and possibly uncompetitive on sparse dual SDPs such as matrix completion (pp. 19-20); future: RBR applied to the same problem (p. 5).

method_links.note: Rank-two structure of a symmetric pair update makes det and inverse updates closed-form, so a coordinate step is O(1) and greedy selection over all pairs is affordable.
Head-to-head comparison on the real goal (ROC against ground truth) rather than equal evaluations; CPU comparison across unequal implementations acknowledged.
Coordinate descent kept; the change is the selection rule and the primal variable space, not a repair.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Iterates of one run at small lambda with decreasing tolerance trace the same TP/FP trade-off as the regularization path.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: convergence by embedding in an existing framework
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Convergence claimed because SINCO is a special case of the RBR method of S048.

transferable: For log-det objectives, keep W = C^{-1} and use the rank-one determinant lemma twice to get a closed-form exact line search along any symmetric pair (pp. 7-8).
If one coordinate step costs O(1), evaluate all candidates and take the best (Gauss-Southwell); cost per iteration stays at the O(p^2) inverse update (pp. 5, 9).
For structure recovery, plot the ROC of one run's iterates at decreasing tolerance next to the ROC of the lambda path (pp. 12-13).
Report CPU time per nonzero when the solution size changes with tolerance (Fig. 3, p. 14).

quotes.text: But since the real goal is to recover true nonzero structure of the covariance matrix, it is not necessary to solve problem (8) accurately.
On the other hand, it may suffer from introducing too few nonzeros and thus missing some of the true positives, especially on denser networks.

title: Efficient Algorithms for the Group Lasso
contribution: Derives an exact block coordinate descent for the Group Lasso without orthonormal groups (each block solved as a trust-region subproblem by Newton's method on the secular equation), a block-step ISTA variant (ISTA-BC) and a hybrid, proves global convergence by embedding both step types in Tseng-Yun BCGD, and shows competitive performance including on MMV problems; the text file is a later revision titled Efficient Block-coordinate Descent Algorithms for the Group Lasso.
problem_entry: Classical BCD for the Group Lasso needs orthonormal group blocks for closed-form updates, and gradient methods (ISTA/FISTA, SLEP) have good rates but are often slower in practice (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: A nonzero block solution solves a trust-region subproblem for some radius, found by Newton on 1 - 1/||y(Delta)|| with a cached eigendecomposition (BCD-GL); for large groups use separate backtracking steps per block (ISTA-BC); switch per group at 200 variables (BCD-HYB); in MMV the block Hessians are multiples of I and both coincide in closed form (pp. 3-7, 12).
assumptions: Least-squares loss, given non-overlapping groups (overlap by column duplication, p. 14); M_j + delta I if M_j singular to meet framework bounds (p. 10).
proof_devices: Beck-Teboulle O(1/k) proof with a vector of block Lipschitz constants replacing the scalar, constant proportional to sqrt(max/min block Lipschitz ratio) (Theorem 1, Lemma 1, pp. 8-9)
global convergence by showing ISTA-BC steps (H_jj = I/t_j) and BCD-GL steps (H_jj = M_j) satisfy Tseng-Yun BCGD's modified Armijo rule and uniform Hessian bounds (Theorem 2, pp. 9-10)
experiments: Matlab; 11 small and 7 large-group synthetic sets, breast-cancer data with 878 overlapping pathway groups, MMV and scalability sets; baselines FISTA, SLEP, BCGD, SpaRSA, SPG/SPOR-SPG; all stopped at F - F* <= 1e-5 vs an ISTA-BC reference; CPU, iterations and fractional Aprods; performance profiles (pp. 13-20).
positioning: Extends Yuan-Lin BCD beyond orthonormal blocks and Beck-Teboulle ISTA/FISTA to per-block steps; convergence via Tseng-Yun BCGD; notes M-BCD appeared concurrently (pp. 2-3, 9-10, 12).
writing: Contribution paragraph enumerates the algorithms (p. 2); results summarised with performance profiles (p. 16); limitations appear inside the method sections, and the conclusion only restates results (pp. 6-7, 21).
limits_future: No rate for ISTA-BC or BCD-GL (p. 7); unclear whether acceleration helps in block form (p. 7); Gauss-Seidel steps not parallel (p. 6); poor on Nemirovski sets (p. 16); Aprods exclude eigendecomposition costs (p. 16); no future work stated (p. 21).

method_links.note: One eigendecomposition per group reused every iteration; identity block Hessians in MMV give closed-form steps.
ISTA kept with only the step rule changed per block; convergence obtained by showing new steps are instances of an existing convergent method (BCGD).
All solvers run to the same objective gap against a common reference, work counted in matrix-vector products; not function evaluations and eigendecomposition cost excluded.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: convergence by embedding in an existing framework
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: BCD-GL and ISTA-BC steps shown to be BCGD steps satisfying its Armijo rule and Hessian bounds, so Tseng-Yun's convergence theorem applies.
Reports that ISTA-BC, ISTA-MS and BCGD do much worse on the Nemirovski worst-case-style sets.

transferable: Solve a group-lasso block exactly as a trust-region subproblem: Newton on 1 - 1/||y(Delta)|| with a cached eigendecomposition (pp. 3-4).
Get global convergence of a hybrid method by showing each step type meets the acceptance rule and Hessian bounds of an existing convergent framework (pp. 9-10).
Count block-wise products as fractions of a full product to keep work comparisons fair (p. 15).
Stop all competitors at the same objective gap against a precomputed reference and report performance profiles (pp. 15-16).

quotes.text: The proofs of the theoretical rates of convergence of the ISTA/FISTA algorithms do not readily extend to ISTA-BC or BCD-GL.
However, as we show in our computational results, the BCD approach (when it can be applied) often outperforms the existing gradient-based approaches.

title: Fast first-order methods for composite convex optimization with line search
contribution: not read: the text file is byte-identical (same MD5) to S028's file, i.e. the FoCM 2014 version with backtracking and X. Bai as coauthor; the 2011 preprint with line search is not in the corpus.
coauthors: D. Goldfarb (as listed; file shows D. Goldfarb and X. Bai)

title: Block coordinate descent methods for semidefinite programming
contribution: Handbook chapter that re-presents the row-by-row BCD method for SDP within a survey of BCD and first-order SDP methods, derives the glasso/Banerjee BCD as RBR on the sparse inverse covariance dual, generalizes RBR to rank-two updates with an SOC positivity condition, and adds comparisons with SDPLR, FPCA and SVT.
problem_entry: Same IPM-cost entry as S048, now with an explicit scope limit that BCD is not a general-purpose SDP solver (p. 2), and RBR placed within surveys of BCD rules/convergence and first-order SDP methods (pp. 2-5).
key_idea: RBR plus two extensions: sparse inverse covariance BCD as RBR on the bound-constrained dual with a Lasso-dual row subproblem (pp. 13-14), and rank-two updates X + (uv^T + vu^T)/2 whose positive definiteness is one SOC constraint in v for fixed u (pp. 21-23).
assumptions: Theorem 3 with explicit compact level set and differentiable convex f (pp. 14-15); AL convergence stated for a slightly modified algorithm with details deferred to Wen's thesis (p. 19); rank-two convergence only sketched for finite spanning direction sets (p. 23).
proof_devices: same Bertsekas-style limit-point argument as S048 Theorem 3.4 (p. 15)
eigenvalues of a rank-two perturbation of the identity give the SOC condition 2 + u^T X^{-1} v - sqrt((u^T X^{-1} u)(v^T X^{-1} v)) > 0 (p. 22)
experiments: Maxcut vs DSDP and SDPLR (SDPLR 4.4e-6-6.9e-5 rel-obj in 4.0-123.9 s vs PURE-RBR-M 2.9e-5-4.9e-5 in 3.9-265.7 s); matrix completion p = q = 200-500 vs FPCA and SVT, with LMaFit named as consistently much faster (pp. 23-26).
positioning: Surveys BCD convergence theory (Bertsekas to Nesterov's RCDM) and first-order SDP methods; credits Banerjee et al. with the first BCD for SDP; positions RBR as a niche solver (pp. 2-5).
writing: Survey-plus-method chapter that opens with an explicit disclaimer against general-purpose use and closes with a summary dominated by limitations (pp. 2, 28).
limits_future: Best when high accuracy is not needed; only non-coupling constraints handled directly; slow near the cone boundary with tight constraints; pure RBR trapped near the boundary on matrix completion (pp. 25, 28); choice of rank-two directions left for further study (p. 23).

method_links.note: Scope rule stated: RBR works when the block subproblem is closed-form or a simple QP; generic use discouraged.
Weak: stronger specialized baselines added (SDPLR, FPCA, SVT) and a faster competitor (LMaFit) named; CPU/accuracy, not evaluations.
Augmented Lagrangian wrapper as the classical fix for BCD with coupling constraints; helps even without coupling.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: States BCD is not a good general-purpose SDP solver, names LMaFit as faster, lists limitations in the summary.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: convergence by embedding in an existing framework
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: AL convergence from standard theory for a slightly modified algorithm; rank-two convergence said to extend easily from Theorem 3.

transferable: State in one sentence where the method should not be used, then show where it wins (p. 2).
Generalize a coordinate update to a rank-two update; for fixed u, positive definiteness is one SOC constraint and the Cholesky factor updates in O(n^2) (p. 22).
When a competitor needs tuning, report the settings tried and that it still failed on some problems (p. 26).

quotes.text: We note, however, that using a BCD method as a general purpose SDP solver is not a good idea.
Like all first-order methods, they are best suited to situations where highly accurate solutions are not required.

title: Aligning ligand binding cavities by optimizing superposed volume
contribution: Applies model-based trust-region DFO (DFO-VASP) to superpose ligand binding cavities by maximizing their overlapping volume computed by VASP, with a noise-driven accuracy increase and warm or Latin-hypercube starts, and validates the superpositions on serine protease and enolase superfamilies.
problem_entry: Application pull: atom-based least-squares superposition does not maximize cavity overlap and fails without atomic similarity; the overlap volume is available only as a noisy, derivative-free VASP computation (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Keep the trust-region DFO framework of the Conn-Scheinberg-Vicente book, but when the model reduction is comparable to the noise level of the current VASP resolution, refine the resolution and rebuild the model; start from the backbone superposition or 10 Latin-hypercube points (p. 2).
assumptions: Rigid superposition (rotations and translations); convergence to a local optimum known only without noise; no global guarantee; noise estimate xi_r assumed available, estimation not described (p. 2).
experiments: 14 serine protease and 10 enolase PDB structures; baseline backbone superposition by Ska; visual orientation check (124/136 consistent), intersection volume vs backbone, and statistical tests of volumetric similarity and fragment volume at the 0.05 level; no optimizer baseline, no evaluation counts or run times (pp. 3-4).
positioning: Against atom-correspondence (RMSD) superposition methods in structural bioinformatics; builds on VASP and trust-region DFO from the IDFO book (pp. 1-2).
writing: Application paper for a bioinformatics audience with the optimization described in two paragraphs; the volume claim differs between abstract, Section 4.2 and conclusion (pp. 1, 4-5).
limits_future: 12 enolase pairs misoriented (p. 3); local optima only (p. 2); inconsistent claims on volume gains (pp. 1, 4-5); future applications to binding specificity and protein engineering (pp. 1, 5).

method_links.note: Early heuristic: evaluation accuracy is raised when the predicted decrease reaches the noise level; accuracy tied to progress but without probability or analysis.
Classical trust-region DFO kept; only the noise-corrupted sufficient-reduction check is repaired.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: fidelity knob tied to predicted decrease vs noise
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Lower VASP resolution (less noise) when model reduction is comparable to the noise estimate, then rebuild the model.

transferable: If a simulator has a fidelity knob, raise fidelity only when the model-predicted decrease becomes comparable to the current noise estimate, then rebuild the model (p. 2).
For a nonconvex application objective, compare a domain warm start with a Latin-hypercube multistart (pp. 2, 4).

quotes.text: The essential mechanism of the above algorithm lies in the checking for the sufficient reduction, which is corrupted when the underlying function 𝑓 is computed with noise.
This algorithmic framework has been shown to converge to a local optimal solution in the absence of noise.

title: Efficient quasi-newton proximal method for large scale sparse optimization
contribution: Presents LHAC, a general-purpose proximal quasi-Newton method for l1-regularized problems that uses a compact L-BFGS Hessian to make coordinate-descent subproblem steps O(m), a greedy working set, and prox-parameter backtracking with a sufficient-decrease test, and reports speed-ups over QUIC and GLMNET.
problem_entry: First-order methods are slow locally, while fast second-order solvers (GLMNET, QUIC) depend on the Hessian structure of one loss; aim for a general method that still beats them (p. 1).
key_idea: Quadratic model with B_k = gamma I - Q R Q^T plus prox term, solved inexactly by coordinate descent in O(m) per step; working set = support plus largest subgradient violations; replace line search by increasing the prox parameter until F(x+d) - F(x) <= rho (Q - F(x)) (pp. 2-3).
assumptions: f convex twice differentiable, g with easy scaled prox (p. 1); theory deferred to other work, rate citation broken, working-set rule a heuristic outside the analysis (pp. 1-2).
experiments: C/C++ LHAC vs QUIC on two gene-expression SICS sets (lambda = 0.5) and vs GLMNET on four sparse logistic regression sets, plus a line-search ablation; stop at relative subgradient norm 1e-6; subgradient vs time plots (pp. 3-4).
positioning: General-purpose alternative to specialized second-order solvers GLMNET and QUIC; working-set idea borrowed from LP and SVM practice (pp. 1-2).
writing: Short paper with a bulleted contribution list (p. 2), theory explicitly deferred, and draft-level artefacts (broken citation, H_k scaling and legend inconsistencies) (pp. 1-4).
limits_future: No theory in this paper; heuristic working set (p. 2); no conclusion section; later analysed in S029 (Math. Program. 2016).

method_links.note: Structure exploited is the low rank of the algorithm's own Hessian approximation, not of f; paper stresses it needs no problem structure.
Classical line search replaced by a trust-region-like prox-parameter update, justified by analysability and performance, with an ablation (same move as S029).
Comparison with specialist solvers on time to a relative subgradient tolerance, not evaluations.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: analysable surrogate for a practical heuristic (c02 candidate)
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Prox-parameter update replaces line search and is claimed to improve performance, with an LHAC vs line-search ablation.

transferable: With a compact L-BFGS matrix, maintain v = Q-hat d so each coordinate step computes (Bd)_i in O(m) (p. 3).
Replace a line search by increasing the prox term and re-solving, accept by a ratio test, and ablate against the line-search version (pp. 3-4).
Build the working set from the current support plus the few largest optimality violations (p. 3).

quotes.text: Instead of line search procedure, we update a prox term of our quadratic model, which allows us to extend global convergence bounds of proximal gradient methods to the case of proximal quasi-Newton methods.
In our experiments small values of ρ provided much better performance than values close to 1.

title: Fast first-order methods for composite convex optimization with backtracking
contribution: Shows that full backtracking (prox parameter allowed to increase) can be used in FISTA and FALM while preserving O(sqrt(L/eps)) complexity, by coupling the momentum update to the ratio of consecutive prox parameters, and gives bounds in terms of the average of square roots of prox parameters or local composite Lipschitz constants.
problem_entry: FISTA's analysis requires nonincreasing prox parameters, so a large early Lipschitz estimate forces small steps forever and the bound depends on the smallest prox parameter; FALM uses a fixed one (pp. 1-2, 13-14).
key_idea: Set theta_k = mu_k/mu_{k+1} in t_{k+1} = (1 + sqrt(1 + 4 theta_k t_k^2))/2 and recompute t_k, y_k whenever backtracking lowers mu_k (FISTA-BKTR, FALM-BKTR), preserving mu_k t_k^2 >= mu_{k+1} t_{k+1}(t_{k+1}-1); motivate with local composite Lipschitz constants that can be much smaller than L(f) (pp. 4-9, 14).
assumptions: f convex C^{1,1} (Assumption 2.1, p. 2); g convex with easy prox (p. 1); Theorem 3.9 needs each initial trial mu at least 1/L(f,g,y_i) (p. 10).
proof_devices: Beck-Teboulle potential 2 mu_k t_k^2 v_k + ||u_k||^2 nonincreasing under the invariant (Lemma 3.3, pp. 6-7)
induction sqrt(mu_{k+1}) t_{k+1} >= sqrt(mu_{k+1})/2 + sqrt(mu_k) t_k giving mu_k t_k^2 >= (sum sqrt(mu_i)/2)^2 (Lemma 3.7, pp. 9-10)
negative argument: with theta_k < 1 alone, t_{k+1} < theta_k^{1/2} t_k + 1 so t_k cannot grow linearly (p. 8)
Nesterov's counting lemma for backtracking calls with mu^0_k = mu_{k-1}/alpha (Lemma 3.10, p. 11)
experiments: Lasso/compressed sensing (Spear10, Spear3, Bdata1, Sparco3), Huber-smoothed l2 and l2-logistic regression on Optdigits; protocol: iterations and matvecs to beat FISTA(j); SpaRSA and YALL1 at defaults; mu trajectories plotted; failures reported (pp. 17-22).
positioning: Generalizes Beck-Teboulle FISTA and Goldfarb-Ma-Scheinberg FALM; compared with Nesterov's composite method, whose backtracking criterion needs an extra gradient per step (pp. 1-2, 10-11).
writing: Abstract states preserved complexity plus the new average-parameter dependence; heuristics and anomalies reported plainly with investigation deferred (pp. 12, 18); conclusion names the missing iterate analysis (p. 22).
limits_future: Concrete gains from local constants need an analysis of the iterates (p. 22); choosing mu increases from local Lipschitz estimates open (p. 11); increase-every-l-iterations heuristic (p. 12); logistic regression analysis future (p. 22).

method_links.note: FISTA/FALM kept; the first property broken by increasing mu (inequality 3.11) repaired by coupling theta_k to the mu ratio inside backtracking; reused by S068.
Deterministic precursor: complexity expressed through the step-parameter trajectory (sum of sqrt(mu_i)), cf. Heuristic 10.
Common accuracy target per checkpoint (FISTA(j)) and work in matvecs; no evaluations or noise.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Shows that simply allowing theta_k < 1 stops t_k from growing before designing the coupled backtracking.

transferable: Carry theta_k = mu_k/mu_{k+1} into the momentum update and recompute the extrapolated point whenever backtracking lowers mu, so the FISTA invariant holds by construction (pp. 8-9).
Prove mu_k t_k^2 >= (sum sqrt(mu_i)/2)^2 by induction to state the rate via the average sqrt(mu_i) (pp. 9-10).
Benchmark by running the baseline j iterations and reporting each competitor's iterations and matvecs to reach the baseline's best value (p. 17).
Plot the step-parameter trajectory beside the tables to explain iteration savings (Figs. 5.1-5.4, pp. 18-23).

quotes.text: The principal drawback of FISTA compared to the method in [9] is the requirement that the estimates of the Lipschitz constant (or the prox parameters) that are used must be nondecreasing from one iteration to the next.
Ideally, one should select the increase of the prox term based on the estimated increase of the local Lipschitz constant.
